concept.name: Mark-to-market
concept.definition: The practice of valuing positions and accounts at current market prices (fair value) rather than historical cost, recognizing gains and losses as prices change; in futures markets it is performed daily or more often and drives variation margin flows.
concept.intuition: Your account reflects what positions are worth now, not what you paid: profits and losses become real every day, not just when you sell.
concept.mechanics: At each settlement the clearinghouse reprices positions to the current settlement price and credits or debits the change; accounts whose balance falls below maintenance margin must be topped up. In accounting, fair-value frameworks (FAS 157 / ASC 820, IFRS 13) formalize exit-price valuation with a hierarchy of input reliability.
concept.formula: Daily P/L credited = (settlement_t - settlement_{t-1}) * multiplier * contracts; account equity_t = equity_{t-1} + daily P/L.
concept.failure_modes: For illiquid or model-priced instruments the 'market' mark is really a model mark (mark-to-model), which can flatter risk metrics and collapse on revaluation; in crises, marking to distressed fire-sale prices forces write-downs and margin calls that feed the spiral — the core of the 2008 fair-value debate.
concept.misconceptions: Mark-to-market does not create losses — it reveals them on schedule rather than at sale — and marking an illiquid asset 'to market' can embed significant estimation discretion despite the name.
concept.example: A trader long a contract marked up 10 points at settlement sees the gain credited in cash that day; a 10-point mark-down the next day is debited, and if the balance then breaches maintenance margin, a margin call follows.
